jurisdictional_context:
Post-separation child contact across the Middle East and Türkiye is governed primarily by personal-status law rather than by a unified civil family code. In the Gulf states, custody (hadanah) and guardianship (wilayah) are allocated under federal or national personal-status statutes — the UAE Federal Decree-Law No. 41 of 2024, the Saudi Personal Status Law of 2022 and their analogues — and disputes normally pass through a court-annexed family guidance or reconciliation stage before litigation. In Lebanon, personal-status matters including custody sit with the recognised religious-community courts rather than with a civil family court, so custody ages and procedure differ by community. In Jordan, Sharia courts hold personal-status jurisdiction for Muslims and church courts for Christians, with court-annexed reconciliation offices attached to the Sharia courts. Türkiye, by contrast, applies a civil code: the Turkish Civil Code governs custody (velayet) and the child's personal relationship with the non-resident parent, and Law no. 7343 of 2021 moved enforcement of handover and contact orders away from coercive execution proceedings to judicial support and victim services directorates operating child meeting centres. Israel applies civil family-court jurisdiction alongside religious courts for personal status.

The consequence for this directory is that the documented actors in most of the region are institutions rather than individually published clinicians: statutory family guidance sections, ministry-run contact and handover centres, professional regulators and national family councils. Extensive searching in English and Arabic located no psychologist, psychiatrist, social worker or family therapist in the six Gulf jurisdictions with a public, citable body of work on parental alienation or contact refusal, and none in Jordan; those jurisdictions are represented institutionally, which reflects what is publicly documented rather than the level of clinical activity.

Israel and Türkiye are the two jurisdictions in this file with a developed professional literature. Israel has an explicit, documented professional exchange on contact refusal (סרבנות קשר) and parental alienation (ניכור הורי): the Rackman Center's 2020 position paper, with a signed expert opinion by a child psychiatrist appended, and a published rebuttal by a university academic writing with a retired family-court judge. Both sides are entered here from their own documents. Türkiye has a Turkish-language literature originating in a 2011 psychiatric review and extending to peer-reviewed survey work with targeted parents, alongside social-work research into how family-court experts encounter the construct in practice.
structural_findings: 15 verified entries across Türkiye, Israel, Lebanon, Jordan, the UAE, Qatar and Saudi Arabia. Stance distribution: recognition 4, middle 1, critique 2, institutional 8. The institutional majority is a finding about what is publicly documented in the region, not a judgement about clinical practice.

Egypt is deliberately NOT in this file. Its entry (eg.nccm, the National Council for Childhood and Motherhood) remains in africa.json, where it was first published. WHO's EMRO region straddles North Africa and the Middle East, and moving the entry would have broken an existing cross-link ID for no reader benefit.

Gulf states (UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain, Oman): no named clinician met the directory standard. Searches in English and in Arabic (التنفير الوالدي / الاغتراب الوالدي) across indexed literature, Gulf university faculties and conference programmes returned no psychologist, psychiatrist, social worker or family therapist with a public, citable body of relevant work. The four Gulf entries are therefore statutory bodies, each verified from its own published materials. Kuwait's Ministry of Justice Family Consultations Department was verified to the same standard and is queued for the next pass.

Türkiye: no critique-camp voice was located. The Turkish-language literature found is recognition-leaning or descriptive, and no Turkish women's-rights or domestic-violence body with a published position on the construct surfaced. This is recorded as a search gap, not as a claim about Turkish professional consensus.

Israel is the only jurisdiction here with both camps documented in their own words, through a traceable 2020 exchange: the Rackman Center position paper (with Dr Flashman's signed expert opinion appended) and the Marcus / Kibenson Bar-On rebuttal. Entries state each party's own position only; neither side's characterisation of the other is reproduced as fact. A forensic-evaluator entry (Prof. Moshe Almagor) was verified but queued for the next pass.

Registration numbers are absent throughout this file. Türkiye operates no single open public register of physician titles, psychologists or social workers; Lebanon publishes no searchable physician index; and the Israeli Ministry of Health practitioners register and the social workers register are JavaScript applications that resisted automated retrieval. Each entry states what was and was not confirmed rather than implying a register check that did not happen.

One named Lebanese clinician, first author of the only Lebanon-specific parental-alienation publication located, was held back from publication because no Lebanese register permits licensure verification and the stance label was genuinely arguable between recognition and middle on the paper's own wording. The draft is retained internally for a later pass.

entries.name: Prof. Dr. Fuat Torun
entries.credentials: Psychiatrist (psikiyatri uzmanı); author-affiliation on 2021-2023 peer-reviewed international papers: Department of Psychiatry, Istanbul Yeni Yüzyıl University School of Medicine. His own official site states associate professorship (doçent) from 2013 and professorship from 2019. entries.affiliation: Department of Psychiatry, Istanbul Yeni Yüzyıl University School of Medicine (affiliation as printed on his 2021 American Journal of Family Therapy and 2023 Journal of Family Issues papers); private psychiatric/psychotherapy practice, Istanbul; previously University of Health Sciences Ümraniye Training and Research Hospital (per his own CV page)
entries.stance_notes: Torun is the earliest and most sustained Turkish-language author on parental alienation: his 2011 review in Psikiyatride Güncel Yaklaşımlar introduced the construct to Turkish psychiatric literature and he authored the Turkish monograph 'Ebeveyne Yabancılaşma Sendromu' (Psikonet, 2017). He uses the syndrome framing while expressly recording the dispute over it — his own 2011 abstract states: 'Birçok araştırmacı çocuklardaki bu yabancılaşmaya ebeveyn yabancılaştırma sendromu kavramını kullanmaktadır. Buna karşın bu kavramın geçerliği üzerindeki tartışmalar halen devam etmektedir.' ('Many researchers use the concept of parental alienation syndrome for this alienation in children. However, debates about the validity of this concept are still ongoing.') His stated purpose there is to describe the presentation, set out the differential diagnosis against abuse, and convey the validity debate to health professionals. His later empirical work with targeted parents in Türkiye (American Journal of Family Therapy 2022; Journal of Family Issues 2023, with S. D. Torun and M. Matthewson) treats parental alienation as a researchable phenomenon and reports targeted parents' own view that professionals lack sufficient knowledge of it. Classified recognition on the strength of that published body of work, with the validity debate acknowledged in his own words rather than dismissed.

entries.stance_notes: Torun is an epidemiologist and public-health physician who co-authored the two peer-reviewed survey studies of targeted parents in Türkiye, with Fuat Torun and Mandy Matthewson. Both papers treat parental alienation as a measurable exposure and report findings in the targeted parents' own terms; the Journal of Family Issues abstract states in the authors' own words that 'Targeted fathers reported lower beliefs in a just world than non-targeted fathers' and that 'Targeted fathers who reported that mental health and legal professionals have sufficient knowledge of parental alienation had higher belief in a just world scores than targeted parents who believed professionals have insufficient knowledge.' Her Yeditepe faculty page lists both parental-alienation papers among her selected publications. Classified recognition on the basis of this published empirical work; she is a public-health researcher rather than a family-court clinician, and no statement by her on the diagnostic status of the construct was located.

entries.stance_notes: Karataş co-authored (with his doctoral student Görkem Yurdakul Muncuk) a qualitative study of how social workers attached to the family courts at the Ankara and Ankara West courthouses view parental alienation, drawn from a 2022 Hacettepe master's thesis he supervised. The authors' own conclusion is cautiously worded rather than diagnostic: 'Çocuğun bir ebeveyni yüzünden diğer ebeveyniyle olan ilişkisini sonlandırması duygusal istismar olabilmekle birlikte çocuğun gelişim sürecinin olumsuz etkilenmesine yol açabilmektedir.' ('A child ending the relationship with one parent because of the other may amount to emotional abuse, and can also lead to the child's developmental process being adversely affected.') They report that court social workers meet such cases frequently but that 'sosyal hizmet müdahalesinin sınırlı olduğu' (social work intervention is limited), and recommend securing the child's participation, careful analysis of family dynamics, an individualised intervention plan for each family and an interdisciplinary approach. Classified middle: the work engages the construct as encountered in Turkish family-court practice and is framed around professional-role limits and the child's best interests rather than around endorsing or rejecting a syndrome.

entries.name: Dr Inbal Kibenson Bar-On
entries.credentials: Doctorate (titled 'ד"ר' on her own signed publication); stated affiliation: Department of Counseling and Human Development, University of Haifa
entries.affiliation: Department of Counseling and Human Development, University of Haifa (as printed on her own September 2020 paper)
entries.stance_notes: Co-author, with retired Jerusalem family court judge Philip Marcus, of a September 2020 critical review titled 'כישלון קשר ילד-הורה: סיבות, אבחון, וטיפול בישראל' ('Child-parent contact failure: causes, diagnosis and treatment in Israel'), written as a response to the Rackman Center position paper. Her stance is recognition-camp but explicitly differentiating rather than absolutist: the paper opens by listing multiple possible causes of contact breakdown, expressly including adolescent rebellion, rejection of the child by the parent, 'תגובת הילד להתעללות בו או בבן משפחתו על ידי ההורה שנדחה' ('the child's reaction to abuse of the child or a family member by the rejected parent'), parental mental illness and addiction, alongside conduct by one parent that causes the child to end contact with the other. The authors accept that the term is contested and often misused — 'קיימת כיום נטייה... לעשות שימוש מוגבר ונרחב במונח ניכור הורי כדרך לבטא כל קושי בקשר' ('there is today a tendency to make increased and expansive use of the term parental alienation as a way of expressing any difficulty in contact') — and argue for distinguishing alienation from other variants of contact breakdown: 'אנו רואים חשיבות רבה לעריכת הבחנה בין ניכור הורי לווריאציות אחרות של ניתוק קשר'. Where a parent causes unjustified severance, they characterise it as 'התעללות פסיכולוגית בילד' ('psychological abuse of the child').

entries.name: Dana Klimi
entries.credentials: Clinical social worker (עו"ס קלינית); certified couples and family therapist; certified supervisor (as listed on her professional directory profile)
entries.affiliation: Director, Michael Center — the external therapeutic and consulting unit of the Neve Michael emergency centres for children and adolescents (Emunah); private clinic, Kibbutz Megiddo
entries.stance_notes: Klimi treats parental alienation and contact breakdown as a clinical phenomenon requiring structured intervention, writing in her own July 2021 article that 'משפחות החוות גירושין עתירי קונפליקט מגיעות לעתים למצבי ניכור הורי ונתק בקשר של הילדים עם אחד ההורים, המעוררים מצוקה ופוגעים בילדים בטווח הארוך' ('families experiencing high-conflict divorce sometimes reach states of parental alienation and severed contact between the children and one parent, which cause distress and harm children in the long term'). Her companion article sets out a 'driving force' model that she describes as 'מודל מערכתי המשלב בין רכיבים ותובנות הלקוחים מהגישות מוכרות לטיפול במצבי ניכור הורי' ('a systemic model combining components and insights drawn from established approaches to treating parental alienation'), distinguishing three types of case by their primary driver: narcissistic injury, anxiety-symbiosis, and deficits arising from parental dysfunction. The formulation is treatment-oriented and differentiating by driver rather than framed as a single syndrome; no statement was located in which she addresses the construct-validity debate directly.

entries.name: Dr Alan (Aharon) Flashman, MD
entries.credentials: MD (New York University); BA (Columbia University); residency training in paediatrics, general psychiatry and child psychiatry, Albert Einstein College of Medicine, New York; recognised in Israel as a specialist in child and adolescent psychiatry (all per his own signed curriculum vitae appended to his February 2020 expert opinion)
entries.affiliation: Private practice in child psychiatry and general psychiatry, Be'er Sheva (since 1983, per his own signed CV); formerly acting director, Child Psychiatry Unit, Soroka Medical Centre, Be'er Sheva; former teaching roles in mental health at Ben-Gurion University of the Negev, the Hebrew University of Jerusalem and Tel Aviv University
entries.stance_notes: Flashman's position is stated in a signed expert opinion (chavat da'at mumche) dated February 2020, prepared at the request of Prof. Ruth Halperin-Kaddari and appended in full to the Rackman Center position paper on contact refusal and parental alienation. He writes that there is no accepted scientific body of knowledge underpinning the proposed syndrome: 'אין גוף ידע מדעי שמקובל בעיני רוב המומחים בתחום שמבסס את התסמונת' ('there is no body of scientific knowledge accepted by most experts in the field that establishes the syndrome'). He separately writes that children may refuse contact for reasons belonging to the relationship with that parent alone and not necessarily through the fault of the other parent. His stated conclusion is procedural rather than absolute: 'מינוי "מומחה לניכור הורי" אינו שומר על ניטרליות אלא מכריע את הכף בטרם עת' ('appointing an "expert in parental alienation" does not preserve neutrality but rather tips the scales prematurely'), adding that any court-appointed expert may address PAS as they see fit. In an August 2023 Times of Israel blog post under his own byline he writes that Gardner's theory 'has been dismissed by medical, psychiatric and psychological associations' and describes its application in Israeli family courts in strongly critical terms.

entries.name: The Ruth and Emanuel Rackman Center for the Advancement of the Status of Women, Bar-Ilan University
entries.credentials: Founded 2001 within the Faculty of Law, Bar-Ilan University; academic legal centre combining research, individual legal representation and policy advocacy in Israeli family law; publishes position papers addressed to decision-makers and submits comments to Knesset committees
entries.stance_notes: Institutional critique anchor for the Israeli contact-refusal debate, justified from the Center's own April 2020 position paper 'סרבנות קשר וניכור הורי: רקע תאורטי, אבחון ושיטות טיפול בראי עיקרון טובת הילד' ('Contact refusal and parental alienation: theoretical background, diagnosis and treatment methods in light of the best-interests-of-the-child principle'), authored by Adv. Avishag Uzrad, Prof. Ruth Halperin-Kaddari and Adv. Osnat Prince. The paper argues that the rise in use of the term in litigation does not necessarily indicate a rise in the phenomenon itself, and that no such treatment speciality exists: 'לא קיימת בעולם הטיפול מומחיות בניכור הורי - לא בתחום הפסיכולוגיה ולא בתחום העבודה הסוציאלית' ('no expertise in parental alienation exists in the treatment world — neither in psychology nor in social work'), noting that parental alienation is absent from the closed statutory lists of recognised specialisations under the Psychologists Regulations 1979 and the social-work expertise rules. It further objects to the same professional serving as both diagnostician and treating clinician, and to coercive remedies such as forced custody transfer and out-of-home placement. The Center states that it acts as an organisation providing legal advice and representation to women in family law, and that the material was also placed before the Supreme Court in an application to join as amicus curiae.

entries.credentials: Statutory body of the T.C. Adalet Bakanlığı (Ministry of Justice), established by the Presidential Decree on Support for Victims of Crime published 10 June 2020. Its Çocuk Hizmetleri Daire Başkanlığı (Child Services Department) is responsible for activities relating to the execution of judgments and interim measures on child handover and the establishment of personal relationship with the child.
entries.affiliation: T.C. Adalet Bakanlığı (Republic of Türkiye, Ministry of Justice); local Adli Destek ve Mağdur Hizmetleri Müdürlükleri in courthouses nationwide
entries.stance_notes: This is the statutory body that now carries out contact and handover orders in Türkiye, and is the institutional anchor for the 2021-2023 reform of that process. Law no. 7343 (Official Gazette, 30 November 2021, no. 31675) amended the Child Protection Law no. 5395 so that, in the Directorate's own words, 'daha önce icra yoluyla zorla yerine getirilen çocuk teslimi veya çocukla kişisel ilişki kurulmasına dair ilâm veya tedbir kararları, artık belirlenen teslim mekânlarında adli destek ve mağdur hizmetleri müdürlükleri ... tarafından yerine getirilmektedir' ('judgments or interim measures on child handover or the establishment of personal relationship with the child, previously enforced coercively through execution proceedings, are now carried out by the judicial support and victim services directorates at designated handover venues'). The implementing regulation was published on 4 August 2022 (Official Gazette no. 31913); the new procedure began in 11 provincial centres on 4 April 2022 and applied nationwide from 8 May 2023. The published guidance states that operations take place in child-friendly 'çocuk görüşme merkezleri' (child meeting centres) through uzmanlar (experts), that they are conducted 'daha çok rızaya dayalı olarak' (mostly on a consensual basis) with contact first established with the parties and the children, that counselling on parenting roles is offered where needed, and that no fee is charged. The Directorate does not use the vocabulary of parental alienation; its framing is the constitutional and Civil Code right of the child to personal and direct contact with both parents and the çocuğun üstün yararı (best interests of the child) standard. Listed as the institutional entry for Türkiye on that basis.

entries.verification_notes: The official site confirms the body's name, its place within the Ministry of Justice, its Child Services Department's remit over child handover and personal-relationship orders, and the postal address, telephone number and email reproduced above. The December 2023 guide PDF was downloaded and its text extracted locally; the Turkish passages quoted are verbatim from the Minister's foreword and the Directorate's preface, which also give the Law no. 7343 Official Gazette reference (30 November 2021, no. 31675), the implementing regulation (4 August 2022, no. 31913), the 4 April 2022 start in 11 provincial centres and the 8 May 2023 nationwide roll-out. The guide names its academic and departmental authors and carries the standard disclaimer that the views expressed are the authors' own and do not reflect the official position of the Ministry, UNICEF Türkiye or Başkent University CEKAMER; the legislative and procedural facts cited here are taken from the official foreword and the Directorate's own web pages rather than from the authored chapters. Where no such directorate exists locally, the orders are executed by civil-court clerk offices designated by the Ministry.

entries.name: Lebanese Order of Psychologists (LOPsy) / نقابة النفسانيين في لبنان
entries.credentials: Statutory professional order for psychologists and psychotherapists in Lebanon. Its own About page states that 'law no. 8 was issued on February 10 of 2017 making it mandatory for practicing psychologists to join the order and earn a professional license after', and that the Order manages its affairs 'in accordance with the rules stipulated in the law no. 254/2022'. Its Resources page publishes both texts as 'Law 8: licensure - القانون ٨/٢٠١٧: تنظيم مهنة النفساني في لبنان' and 'Law 254: creation of the Lebanese order of Psychologists - القانون ٢٥٤: انشاء نقابة النفسانيين في لبنان'.
entries.affiliation: Lebanese Order of Psychologists; licensing operated with the Ministry of Public Health (work permit committee) and the Ministry of Education and Higher Education (colloquium exam committee), per the Order's own history page
entries.stance_notes: Included as the Lebanese regulatory anchor rather than for any position on the PA construct: no PA-specific, contact-refusal-specific or custody-specific statement by the Order was located in its published legal documents, guidelines or site pages. The Order operates a public professional directory (1,882 listed licensed professionals at the time of checking), filterable by licence type (Clinical / Educational), psychotherapy specialisation and a 'Child and Adolescent' sub-specialty, which makes it the practical licensure-verification route for named Lebanese psychologists. Its published 'LOPsy Guidelines for Assessments and Evaluations' address assessment competence generally and instruct that 'Psychologists strive to consider the multiple and global settings (e.g., forensic, education, integrated care) in which services are being provided', without addressing custody or child-contact evaluation specifically. In a country where personal-status matters sit with recognised religious-community courts, the Order states that its 'activities are purely professional, free from any partisan, ideological or religious commitment'. Country_code: LB.
entries.verification_notes: The public directory at https://lopsy.org/members was opened and is searchable via a 'search' query parameter; it reported 1,882 matches unfiltered at the time of checking. The guidelines PDF was downloaded and read in full text. No registration numbers are displayed in the directory, so none is recorded here. A Ministry of Public Health news listing carries a headline referring to a Lebanese Order of Psychologists 'Forum on the Contemporary Family'; the article body could not be retrieved and nothing about that forum is asserted in this entry.

entries.name: National Council for Family Affairs (NCFA) / المجلس الوطني لشؤون الأسرة
entries.credentials: Established by Law No. 27 of 2001. Its own About page states: 'تأسس المجلس الوطني لشؤون الأسرة بموجب قانون رقم 27 لعام 2001 برئاسة جلالة الملكة رانيا العبدالله المعظمة' — 'The National Council for Family Affairs was established under Law No. 27 of 2001, chaired by Her Majesty Queen Rania Al Abdullah.'
entries.affiliation: National Council for Family Affairs, Jordan
entries.stance_notes: Jordan's statutory umbrella and coordinating body for family policy, included for its documented role in family counselling and child protection rather than for any position on the PA construct, which was not located in its published material. Its About page describes the Council as working 'كمظلة داعمة للتنسيق وتيسير عمل الشركاء من المؤسسات الوطنية الحكومية وغير الحكومية والمؤسسات الدولية والقطاع الخاص العاملة في مجال الأسرة' — 'as a supporting umbrella for coordinating and facilitating the work of partners from national governmental and non-governmental institutions, international institutions and the private sector working in the field of the family.' Its published studies list includes an evaluative study of family counselling centres (الدراسة التقييمية لمراكز الإرشاد الأسري, 2019) and a national study on violence against children in Jordan (2019-2020), placing post-separation family counselling and child protection within its documented remit. No statement on parental alienation, contact refusal or post-separation child contact was located. Country_code: JO.

entries.name: Supreme Judge Department — Family Reconciliation, Mediation and Conciliation Offices / دائرة قاضي القضاة — مكاتب الإصلاح والوساطة والتوفيق الأسري
entries.credentials: Government department administering Jordan's Sharia courts. The official General Budget Department chapter for the Supreme Judge Department gives its legal framework as 'Sharia Courts Formation Law No.(19) of 1972 and amendments thereto, and Supreme Judge Department's Administrative Organization bylaw No. (18) of 1993 and amendments thereto', and its mission as 'Achieving justice in the community, preserving the rights of women and children, protecting the family and disseminating the Sharia and legal culture.'
entries.affiliation: Supreme Judge Department (دائرة قاضي القضاة), Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan; offices attached to Sharia courts
entries.stance_notes: Jordan's court-annexed family conciliation and counselling service, included for its documented role in family disputes handled by the Sharia courts rather than for any position on the PA construct, which does not appear in its published material. The official budget chapter for the Department lists, among its stated priority outcomes, 'Increase the numbers of family reform offices', 'Institutionalize guidance and advocacy work in family reform offices', 'Promote relationships with the partner sectors in the guidance field and family rehabilitation', 'Promote relationship with human, family and child rights organizations' and 'Contribute to promoting the family cohesion', and it reports a performance measure for the 'Number of rehabilitation and family guidance centers'. The Department's own website carries a section headed 'الإصلاح والوساطة والتوفيق الأسري' (family reconciliation, mediation and conciliation) linking to a 'مديرية الإصلاح والتوفيق الاسري' (Family Reconciliation and Conciliation Directorate). Personal-status jurisdiction in Jordan sits with Sharia courts for Muslims and church courts for Christians; this entry describes the structure factually and takes no position on it. Country_code: JO.

entries.verification_notes: The General Budget Department PDF was downloaded and read as text; all quoted phrases are verbatim from that document, including its own English spelling ('family reform offices'). The Supreme Judge Department website is JavaScript-rendered and largely resists automated retrieval: direct curl returned a 118-byte response and a reader proxy returned only accessibility chrome, but a fetch of pageID=200 confirmed the page is titled 'الإصلاح والوساطة والتوفيق الأسري - دائرة قاضي القضاه' and displays a link labelled 'مديرية الإصلاح والتوفيق الاسري'. No staffing composition, qualification requirements or custody/visitation role of these offices was confirmed from a primary source, and none is asserted. Jordanian broadcaster Al Mamlaka (8 September 2026) reported, from the annual Sharia courts report, that the offices contributed to preserving the cohesion of more than 9,000 families and converted more than 35,000 cases into consensual agreements during 2025; those figures are secondary reporting and are recorded here only as such.

entries.name: Abu Dhabi Judicial Department (ADJD) — Family Guidance Section / Management of Alternative Solutions to Resolve Disputes
entries.credentials: Emirate-level judicial authority of Abu Dhabi; operates the court-annexed Family Guidance Section, described on ADJD's own page as founded 10 October 1998; family guidance is the statutorily required pre-litigation stage for most personal-status disputes under Article 16 of Federal Law No. 28 of 2005
entries.affiliation: Abu Dhabi Judicial Department, Government of Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates
entries.stance_notes: ADJD's own published Family Guidance Program booklet states that for the majority of personal-status disputes 'the court cannot be approached directly and instead the parties must first attend family guidance, according to Article 16 of Federal Law No. 28 of 2005 concerning personal status matters.' The same booklet describes sessions conducted by an independent third party 'known as the Family Counsellor', and states that where agreement is reached it is 'signed by the family guidance judge; such an agreement shall be treated as a legally binding order which may not be challenged by way of appeal unless it violates the provisions of the law.' ADJD's Family Guidance page lists the section's subject-matter as including 'Custody: Proof of custody, removal of custody, joint custody, visitation of the the children (parenting time)' and 'Rights of the children subject of custody: Child support, housing costs, school fees, custody fees.' Classified institutional as a court-annexed statutory counselling service with a documented role in custody and contact matters; ADJD publishes no position on parental alienation as a clinical construct, and none was located.
entries.contact: https://www.adjd.gov.ae/en/pages/family-guidance.aspx (case registration is electronic; sessions described on ADJD's page as conducted by remote videoconferencing)
entries.verification_notes: Existence and mandate verified directly from two ADJD-operated primary sources: the English Family Guidance page at adjd.gov.ae (HTTP 200 on re-check) and ADJD's own 15-page 'Family Guidance Program — Management of alternative solutions to resolve disputes and family guidance section' booklet hosted at adjd.gov.ae (HTTP 200; PDF downloaded and text extracted locally, quotations above taken verbatim from that extraction). The booklet additionally records that the Family Programme 'is a concept introduced in 2020 by Abu Dhabi Judicial Department; the first of its kind in the GCC region', and that in 2017 ADJD signed an agreement with the Angelical Church and the Orthodox Coptic Church in Abu Dhabi so that non-Muslims may engage in family guidance through those bodies. NOT verified: the number, names, professional qualifications, or health-regulator licensure of individual family guidance counsellors — ADJD's published materials name no individuals and state no licensing requirement, and no counsellor roster was located on any official page. No ADJD publication using the term 'parental alienation' or any Arabic equivalent was located. The booklet carries no printed publication date, so no publication year is asserted here. The Arabic page was retrieved via the r.jina.ai reader proxy because the site is JavaScript-rendered.

entries.name: Federal Judicial Council of the United Arab Emirates (Al-Majlis Al-Qada'i Al-Ittihadi)
entries.credentials: Federal judicial rule-making body of the UAE; issuing authority of the 2025 regulatory decisions implementing Federal Decree-Law No. (41) of 2024 (Federal Personal Status Law), announced through the UAE Ministry of Justice
entries.affiliation: Federal Judicial Council / Ministry of Justice, United Arab Emirates
entries.stance_notes: The UAE Ministry of Justice announced, in an item dated Friday 28 November 2025, that the Federal Judicial Council introduced five new regulatory decisions implementing Federal Decree-Law No. (41) of 2024, the Federal Personal Status Law. On that page the Ministry states that 'Resolution No. (67) of 2025 — Family Guidance Regulation' 'grants family counselors a broader role in resolving disputes amicably and give their agreements the force of an executive deed', and that 'Resolution No. (68) of 2025 — Visitation Regulation' was 'introduced to provide clear legal framework for visitation rules while prioritizing the child's psychological and social well-being.' The official consolidated text of the Personal Status Law on the UAE Legislation portal allocates court competence over, among other matters, 'Custody, visitation, and related issues' (Article 3, Clause 3(b)). Classified institutional: a federal rule-making body whose published instruments govern post-separation child contact and the counsellors who mediate it; it publishes no position on parental alienation as a clinical construct, and none was located.

The text of the Personal Status Law, including the Article 3(3)(b) allocation of competence over 'Custody, visitation, and related issues', was read on the Government of the UAE's official uaelegislation.gov.ae record for the Decree-Law, retrieved via the r.jina.ai reader proxy because the portal is JavaScript-rendered; a direct download of the portal's PDF endpoint returned an HTML shell rather than the document. NOT verified: the full operative text of Resolution No. (67) of 2025 and Resolution No. (68) of 2025 themselves — only the Ministry's own summary of each was located on a government domain, and the summaries are quoted here rather than paraphrased or sharpened. Commercial legal databases render Resolution No. 68 of 2025 under the style 'Federal Administrative Decision No. 68/2025 — On the Visitation Regulation of Children Under Custody'; because that wording was not confirmed on a government source, the Ministry's own styling is used above. No UAE federal instrument or announcement using the term 'parental alienation' or an Arabic equivalent was located.

entries.name: Family Consulting Center (Wifaq) — مركز الاستشارات العائلية (وفاق)
entries.credentials: Private Qatari institution of public interest, established 13 November 2002; supervised by the Qatar Foundation for Social Work; free services launched 24 August 2003; operates a Parental Care Section within its Counseling Department
entries.affiliation: Family Consulting Center (Wifaq), under the Qatar Foundation for Social Work
entries.stance_notes: Wifaq's own site states that the centre was 'established by Her Highness Sheikha Moza Bint Nasser, may God protect her, on 13 November 2002', that it is 'a private Qatari institution of public interest' and that it is 'supervised by the Qatar Foundation for Social Work'. Qatar's official government services portal, Hukoomi, states that the service is delivered by the Parental Care Section of Wifaq's Counseling Department, and that this section 'supervises the mechanism for implementing judicial rulings and judgments and amicable agreements about regulating custodial issues for children of divorcees or children of broken families who have family disputes'; the listed services include 'Providing a safe environment for the child, where the Parental Care Section acts as a link between the child and parents' and 'Preparing and rehabilitating children for the stage that follows the separation or divorce of parents, as well as sparing them the negative effects of divorce.' Wifaq's own services page separately lists a Family Reconciliation Service that handles disputes and mediation in cases 'referred by courts or agencies', alongside psychological consultations and a psychological testing and measurement service. Classified institutional as a court-referral-receiving family counselling body with a documented role in implementing custody and contact arrangements; no Wifaq position on parental alienation as a construct was located.

entries.name: Ministry of Justice (Saudi Arabia) — 'Shaml' centres for enforcing custody, viewing and visitation rulings (مبادرة تنفيذ أحكام الحضانة والرؤية والزيارة «شمل»)
entries.credentials: Initiative of the Saudi Ministry of Justice under the National Transformation Programme / Vision 2030, delivered through specialised centres in partnership with the non-profit sector; listed as a completed initiative on the Ministry's own initiatives register
entries.city: Riyadh (initiative headquarters; centres distributed across the regions of the Kingdom)
entries.affiliation: Ministry of Justice, Kingdom of Saudi Arabia
entries.stance_notes: The Ministry of Justice's own initiatives register describes 'تنفيذ أحكام الحضانة والرؤية والزيارة (شمل)' as an initiative aiming 'to provide a suitable and safe environment for implementing custody, viewing and visitation rulings through specialised centres, in partnership with the non-profit sector', seeking 'to safeguard the rights of the child and preserve the privacy of the family, through providing psychological and social support to the parties concerned' (translation of the Ministry's Arabic text). The Saudi Press Agency records the Minister of Justice launching the initiative on 6 Jumada al-Ula 1441 AH / 1 January 2020 with 19 specialised centres prepared across all regions, stating that it addresses 'the negative psychological and social effects resulting from implementing these rulings in places not prepared for the child' and provides 'social and psychological support to the parties to the dispute (the parents — and the children)' (translation). A later Saudi Press Agency item dated 30 November 2020 reports 21 centres delivering more than 85,000 services to 34,000 beneficiaries annually, and lists among the initiative's aims 'creating a safe and sound environment for handing over the child in custody', 'raising the parents' awareness of the importance of stability after separation', and 'providing assistance to the court in pending cases requiring social and psychological reporting' (translation). Classified institutional as a ministry-run, court-linked service for enforcing contact and handover orders; the Ministry publishes no position on parental alienation as a clinical construct, and none was located.

The launch date, launching minister, initial centre count and operational statistics were verified on two dated Saudi Press Agency items (both HTTP 200 on re-check), SPA being the official state news agency; each SPA item carries its own Hijri and Gregorian date, which is the basis for the publication years given. Arabic originals were read and are translated here; no wording has been strengthened in translation. NOT verified: the current number of operating centres (sources give 19 at launch in January 2020 and 21 as at November 2020, and no later official figure was located), the identity or professional licensure of the social and psychological specialists staffing the centres, and the identity of the non-profit operating partners.
